svg.text: A single spine runs top to bottom through the article's stages — properties, uses, silk types, natural spinning,
artificial synthesis, research, human uses — with the two richest stages (properties, artificial synthesis) drawn
as hubs branching into their sub-topics before the spine continues.

g.text: Spider silk: from biology to imitation
Down the page follows the article's own order; the two hub regions (Properties, Artificial synthesis) are where the
piece has the most going on and open into their own scenes.

g.title: Spider silk: a multipurpose protein fibre — prey capture, shelter, courtship, mobility — Nearly all spiders make silk, even species that build no web at all. — → spya-gp4t9x
Strength, stretch, stickiness — A layered molecular structure gives silk its mix of toughness and give. — → spya-py9zw6
Hard crystals in a stretchy matrix — Stiff beta-sheet crystals sit inside soft, folded protein regions. — → spya-p263u9
Tougher than steel, stretchier too — High strength plus high stretch lets silk absorb huge energy before it snaps. — → spya-nwva2u
Glue that sets on contact — Pyriform silk forms attachment discs that bond instantly and later biodegrade. — → spya-m8z9e7
Many jobs: trapping, escaping, mating — up to 7 silk types per spider — From orb webs to ballooning threads to pheromone-laced trails. — → spya-rty5kb
g.text: up to 7 silk types per spider

g.title: Each gland makes its own silk — dragline, capture-spiral, wrapping, egg case — A silk's job can be traced back to the specific gland that made it. — → spya-hg7j7e
g.text: Each gland makes its own silk

g.title: Pulled, not squeezed out — liquid protein hardens as it's drawn — Spinning is pultrusion: the fibre forms as it is pulled, not pumped out under pressure. — → spya-g3h8qq
g.text: liquid protein hardens as it's drawn

g.title: Copying silk: protein plus machine — Making artificial silk means recreating both the liquid protein and the spinning duct. — → spya-d7d7m8
Borrowed proteins, mixed results — E. coli, silkworms and goats have all been engineered to make silk-like protein. — → spya-rw0wtg
Syringes, microfluidics, electrospinning — Simple protein still needs a duct-like device to become a real fibre. — → spya-x4bwhf
Beyond fibres: capsules, membranes — The same protein can self-assemble into sheets, nanowires and drug capsules. — → spya-r4r9au
Still short of natural silk — Lab-made fibres come out thicker and weaker than a spider's own dragline silk. — → spya-j7hems
Decades of mapping silk's chemistry — From 1960s amino-acid analysis to 2000s X-ray studies of silk as it's spun. — → spya-jvxbb8
From stockings to violin strings — textiles, medicine, optics — Centuries of attempts to harvest spider silk for cloth, wound care and instruments. — → spya-chy97m
References & further reading — Citations, external links and related topics. — → spya-jdybu5

g.text: A hub shape: structural basis above feeds a cluster of five mechanical measures, which funnel down into the separate

g.title: Hard crystal blocks in a soft, stretchy web — Stiff beta-sheet crystals are linked by softer, helix-and-turn regions. — → spya-p263u9
g.text: Hard crystal blocks in a soft, stretchy web

g.title: Strong, stretchy and tough, together — Dragline silk's rare combination of high strength and high stretch. — → spya-nwva2u
Softer, bendier than steel — Silk's Young's modulus is far lower than steel's or Kevlar's — it gives more easily. — → spya-dq9b7q
Near steel, half of Kevlar — Dragline silk's tensile strength rivals high-grade steel. — → spya-mhe2r5
A sixth the density of steel — A silk strand long enough to circle the Earth would weigh about 2 kg. — → spya-hng89u
Matches top synthetic fibres — Dragline silk's toughness rivals the best commercial polyaramid fibres. — → spya-gfykz5
Shrinks and softens when wet — Dragline silk can shrink up to 50% in water, possibly to re-tension webs. — → spya-qdjb0x
Glue that sets on contact, then biodegrades — Attachment-disc silk polymerises immediately and stays usable indefinitely. — → spya-m8z9e7
g.text: Glue that sets on contact, then
Two columns off one starting claim — matching feedstock attempts against matching spinning-duct attempts — converge on
one verdict, with a side note on non-fibre uses.

g.title: Two tasks: make the protein, build the duct — feedstock and spinning conditions — Few strategies so far have managed both well enough to spin usable fibre. — → spya-wgee6t
g.text: Two tasks: make the protein, build the

g.title: Feedstock: borrowed silk proteins — Silk's protein is long and complex, so stand-in organisms are used instead. — → spya-rw0wtg
E. coli-made protein matches real silk — Engineered bacteria produced fibre matching natural dragline silk's strength and stretch. — → spya-f399m7
g.text: E. coli-made protein matches real silk

g.title: Goat milk: silk protein, weaker fibre — Goats secreted silk protein in their milk, but spun fibres fell short of natural silk. — → spya-brz8bx
g.text: Goat milk: silk protein, weaker fibre

g.title: Geometry: copying the spinning duct — Simple protein still needs a duct-like apparatus to become a working fibre. — → spya-x4bwhf
Syringe & needle: cheap, crude — Easy to build, but needs chemicals or stretching to harden the fibre properly. — → spya-y4ay23
Microfluidics: precise, costly — Controllable small-scale spinning, now reaching commercial continuous fibre. — → spya-qbrkma
Also: capsules, membranes, nanowires — The same proteins can self-assemble into shapes besides fibres. — → spya-r4r9au
Close, but still short of natural silk — Artificial fibres end up thicker, weaker and less flexible than a spider's own. — → spya-j7hems
g.text: Close, but still short of natural silk
